sections.title: A Land of Separate Basins

paragraphs.text:
When the civilizations of the Near East were already at their height, the farming peoples along the Yellow River were only beginning the long movement toward civilized life.
Without knowing what would come of it, they were laying the first foundations of the Chinese empire.

paragraphs.text:
Chinese civilization grew with its face turned away from the Mediterranean world.
At first it stood outside that world and knew of it only indirectly, through long prehistoric contacts with the peoples of the Scytho-Siberian zone.
Its real setting was eastern Asia, where mountains and plains descend from the Tibetan plateau toward the Pacific.
There two great zones, divided by immense mountain barriers and watered by great rivers, gave China a broken and compartmented form.
This was never a single open land.
It was a region cut into difficult and often self-contained spaces.

In the north, Shanxi formed one of those enclosed worlds.
Toward the southwest it opened down toward the Yellow River through the lower Fen valley.
But toward the south and east the Taihang and Wutai ranges rose like a wall between plateau and plain.
The Qin valley gave the plateau lords a corridor toward the Henan plain, yet it was a poor road for anyone trying to force a way back upward.
The passes farther northeast were few and hard.
That is why the rulers of Shanxi, the lords of Jin, dealt constantly with powers to the west, but had far less direct intercourse with the east.
When they descended toward the Yellow River plain, they usually did so through the Qin valley and emerged toward what was later called Wei.

At the far western edge of the Chinese world, the Wei valley formed another almost sealed compartment.
To the south the huge Qinling range closed it with a formidable barrier.
To the north and west lived non-Chinese peoples, and beyond them stretched the desert.
Its only connection with the rest of China was the Yellow River.
Yet after the river struck Huashan and turned eastward, it became a poor road, shallow and sand-choked in winter, violent in summer.
Here too geography left a deep mark on history.
The lords of Qin remained somewhat apart from the rest of the Chinese world, yet fought for centuries to seize the opening by which the Yellow River enters the great eastern plain.

Farther south, the Yangtze basin formed another distinct realm.
Its northern boundary was clear enough, but easy access existed mainly along the coast where the Yellow River, the Huai, and the Yangtze had long spread their waters through branching channels.
Beyond that, once the mountains begin, communication narrows sharply.
The Huai ranges were not very high, but their long ridges, abrupt slopes, and endless passes made movement slow and dangerous.
Farther west the routes grew harder still, and the best roads from the Wei valley to the Han valley had to cross passes more than one thousand meters high.
The kings of Chu were thus protected by their own terrain.
They could strike northward into the central plain and then fall back into their own country, where pursuit through the long mountain passes invited ambush.
Only when a strong power rose on the lower Yangtze and turned the line of their defenses did Chu become truly vulnerable.

To the northeast, ancient Qi, in the region of modern Hebei and Shandong, also possessed powerful natural defenses.
To the north and west it was shielded by immense marshes and shifting branches of the lower Yellow River.
To the south stood the Taishan massif, reaching eastward toward the sea.

Only the great eastern plain lacked such shelter.
There communication was easy, waterways crossed everywhere, and no natural obstacle could stop an army for long.
It was rich and fertile, but almost indefensible.
Again and again it became a battlefield ravaged by northern, southern, and western invaders.
The very shape of the land imposed enduring conditions on the history of early China.

sections.title: The Chinese Core and the Surrounding Peoples

paragraphs.text:
The China in which civilization first took shape was far smaller than the China of later ages.
It covered only part of the middle and lower Yellow River basin.
Even there the Chinese were not alone.
The irrigated plains were theirs, but the mountains, even deep inside this world, remained in the hands of non-Chinese peoples.

paragraphs.text:
The terraced plateaus of Shanxi were the land of the Di.
In the south, the six tribes of the Red Di lived in Shangdang and along the upper courses of the Qin and the two Zhang rivers.
One group held the left bank of the Yellow River where the plain narrows into mountain country.
Farther east were others whose names survived in later place names around Lu'an.
Still others occupied the southeastern corner of Shanxi and the country stretching northward toward the river.
North of the Red Di, the White Di held the Wutai massif and the lands below it in modern Hebei.
Their reduction took centuries.
The Red Di were brought under control in the late sixth century BC, but one White Di group endured in the Wutai mountains until almost the end of the Zhou age.

The west and center of Shanxi had been subdued earlier.
Since very ancient times Chinese settlers had occupied the lower Fen valley and founded small principalities there.
At an early date they also gained a foothold in the rich Taiyuan basin.
The mountain Di between the Yellow River and the Fen were thus cut off and eventually brought under control.
Only the tribes farther north remained independent.
They later founded the small kingdom of Dai.
Beyond them, on the rim of the steppe, lived the nomads of the broad Mongolian plateau.
Among these northern peoples were groups later associated with the Xiongnu, as well as eastern peoples near the sea.
Still farther north were communities with no cities, no palaces, no ancestral temples, and only the simplest farming.

The same pattern appeared south and west of the Yellow River, where many surrounding peoples were called Rong.
The mountains between the Luo River and its tributary the Yi were occupied by the Rong of Luo, the Rong of Yi, and other such groups, who dominated the eastern Zhou capital at Luoyi.
Farther southeast, near the northwest reaches of the Huai mountains, lived the Rong Man.
The Wei plain too was ringed by Rong peoples.
On the southern slopes of Huashan lived the Li.
In the mountains of western and northern Shaanxi were many other groups, including the Kunrong, the Mianzhu, the Wushi, and above all the Yiqu, who resisted Chinese expansion for centuries.

Yet enclaves survived inside the plain itself, remnants left behind as the Chinese advance moved westward.

Southward, the Yangtze basin was the realm of the Man.
They came under Chinese pressure only with the conquests of the eleventh century BC.
They soon recovered independence and remained outside full control until the end of the Zhou, becoming civilized more by contact than by conquest.
Along the eastern seacoast and the lower Huai lived the Huai Yi in marshy country.
Farther west were the Xu, who had once occupied much of the land between the Yellow River and the Huai mountains.
By historical times they had been pushed eastward by the lords of Lu and Song, though remnants survived farther west.
The Shandong peninsula also preserved older non-Chinese populations in its mountain districts, even where strongly sinicized principalities later appeared.

Thus the early Chinese sphere was clearly bounded.
It consisted of two chief regions separated by belts of non-Chinese peoples.
The larger lay in the lower Yellow River basin and reached the sea only on a narrow frontage north and south of the Shandong peninsula.
The smaller lay in the plain where the Wei and Luo rivers join the Yellow River, between Huashan and the Shaanxi plateau.

Yet the word barbarian can mislead.
Some of these peoples in the far north may indeed have belonged to northern steppe stocks later associated with Tungusic peoples or the Huns.
Some southern groups may have been related to Tibetan or Miao populations.
But many of the Di, many of the Rong, the Xu, the Huai peoples, and even much of the population of Chu, Wu, and Yue were probably small Chinese kindred groups.
They had remained in mountains, marshes, and forests apart from the civilizing movement that carried the peoples of the plain forward.
The difference was often social more than strictly ethnic.
Writing, political organization, and material development slowly widened that difference.
A Rong chief, as the Zuo zhuan later reports him saying, put it simply.
Our food, our drink, and our clothing are not those of the Chinese states.
We do not exchange their courtesies.
Their language and ours are not understood alike.

notes.title: Rong, Di, and shifting identities
notes.text: Modern scholarship is more cautious than older accounts about treating Rong, Di, Yi, and related labels as fixed ethnic blocs. In early sources they often function as shifting political or cultural designations, and backward identifications with later peoples such as the Xiongnu or Tungusic groups should be treated with care.

sections.title: The Shape of the World Under Heaven

paragraphs.text:
Within all under heaven, the tianxia, China imagined itself as a civilized island in a sea of surrounding peoples.
That political situation helped shape the ancient Chinese picture of the universe.
The world was imagined as a chariot.
The square earth was its body, and the round heaven its canopy.

Heaven rose in nine levels.
Between one level and the next stood guarded gates watched by the servants of the Lord on High, Shangdi.
At the boundary between heaven and earth was the lowest of these gates, through which the west wind descended.
At the highest level, in the region of the Great Bear, stood the Celestial Palace where the Lord on High ruled heaven and earth.
This palace was guarded by the Celestial Wolf, identified with Sirius.
Ancient imagination gave that guardian a terrible grandeur.
He paces softly, seizes men like a toy, and hurls them into a bottomless pit.

The underside of heaven was not conceived as a vault.
It was flat, like a wheel or canopy spread above the earth.
No walls closed the world laterally.
Instead the sky was held up at the eight extremities of the earth by pillars that kept heaven and earth apart.
Once, it was said, those pillars were equal and the two ran level.
Then a cataclysm toppled the northwestern pillar, Mount Buzhou.
Since then heaven has tilted toward the northwest and earth toward the southeast.
That is why the stars move westward through the night and the rivers of the earth flow from west to east.
Across the heavens also ran the Celestial River, the Milky Way, dividing the Weaving Maiden from the Herd Boy.
Other openings in the sky allowed celestial and earthly forces to mix.
There was a Gate of Cold at the north and a Gate of Heat at the south.

The sun and moon were not merely remote bodies in the sky.
The sun, imagined as a fiery blossom, spent the night on earth.
At dawn his mother Xihe bathed him in the Pool of Sweetness.
He then crossed the Valley of Sunrise and climbed the heavens by a vast tree whose branches gave him access to the sky.
In the evening he descended again in the west.
Ancient myth said that Xihe had ten suns, each meant to appear in turn.
Once all ten rose together and the earth began to burn.
Then the great archer Yi shot down nine of them.
The moon too was imagined in multiple forms, twelve daughters who took turns lighting the world.
Eclipses came when monsters attacked sun or moon in mid-course.

Beneath this heaven lay the inhabited earth in concentric zones.
At the center were the Nine Provinces of China, surrounded by the Di, Rong, Man, and Yi.
To the east and south stretched the seas.
To the north lay vast deserts associated with the Lady of Drought.
Beyond the inhabited world flowed the Four Seas, girdling the world much like the Ocean River of Greek imagination.
Outside them lay lands inhabited by gods, goddesses, dwarfs, giants, and monsters.
There lived the deities of the winds, the Count of the Waters, the Queen Mother of the West, and many other beings of the far horizons.
Ancient Chinese fancy placed in these outer lands every kind of marvel, including strange races and colossal creatures.

Farther still were the corners of the earth not covered by the round sky.
In the southwest lay a land where heat and cold, day and night, were scarcely distinguished.
In the northwest lay the land of the Nine Yin, never touched by the sun.
There stood the Torch Dragon, a being with a serpent's body and a human head.
When he opened his eyes it became day.
When he closed them it became night.
His breath made the wind.
His inhaling brought winter, and his exhaling brought summer.
In the southeast yawned the Great Abyss, into which both terrestrial waters and the Milky Way poured without filling it.
Beyond that lay pure void, without earth below or sky above.
Such was the imagined world in which the ancient Chinese gave themselves the place of honor at the center, in Zhongguo, the Middle Country.

sections.title: The People of the Yellow River

paragraphs.text:
What, then, were the Chinese of the Yellow River like in bodily type.
Maspero presents them as not greatly different from their modern descendants in Hebei, Henan, and Shandong.
They were of moderate height but vigorous.
They had straight black hair, prominent cheekbones, somewhat slanting and projecting eyes, a broad mouth, strong teeth set a little apart, and only a scant beard and moustache.

Early literary portraits preserved an ideal of noble appearance.
A distinguished man might be praised for a dragon face, a tiger mouth, protruding ears, large eyes, and widely spaced teeth.
When Chinese writers of the early centuries of the Common Era described such faces, they were describing a type they knew as their own.
That is why later encounters with Buddhist missionaries from India and Iran, men with deep-set eyes and strong noses, could seem so strikingly foreign.

A poem from the seventh century BC shows that the feminine ideal was not far from what later Chinese taste would admire.
A girl's fingers are likened to fresh white shoots.
Her skin is like frozen cream.
Her neck is like a white grub.
Her teeth are like melon seeds.
Her brow is like a cicada's head.
Her eyebrows are like silkworm feelers.
Her black hair is like clouds.
Her smile makes her teeth shine.
Tall men were not unknown either.
The father of Confucius was said to be very large, and Confucius himself inherited something of that imposing stature.
In this respect too, the people of the ancient north seem to stand close to the people later seen in the same countryside.

sections.title: Language and Southern Affinities

paragraphs.text:
A common theory held that the Chinese were originally a branch of the northern nomadic peoples who settled on the Yellow River and became civilized there.
Maspero argues that, whatever their remote blood may have been, the affinities of their earliest culture point in another direction.
Chinese, he says, has no real relation to the languages of the northern tribes.
Its nearest affinities lie rather with the Tai languages of the south and, less clearly but still significantly, with the Tibeto-Burman world.

notes.title: Language classification
notes.text: Maspero's Sino-Tai grouping is no longer standard. Chinese is now generally treated as part of Sino-Tibetan, while Tai-Kadai is usually classified separately; proposals for a deeper relationship remain debated.

paragraphs.text:
From the earliest stage that can be traced, this Sino-Tai group already shows the traits later associated with Chinese.
Words are monosyllabic.
Clusters of consonants are sharply limited.
Final consonants are few.
Diphthongs and triphthongs are common.
Above all, tone is one of the essential features of the system.
Words do not inflect.
They do not change form through endings or conjugations.
Older traces of derivation may once have existed in prefixes, tonal alternations, and reduplication, but by historical times these devices had only weak remnants left.
Because nouns and verbs were often not distinguished by form, syntax had to remain strict, and meaning depended heavily on position and on particles.

Language was not the only sign pointing southward.
Ancient Chinese civilization was agricultural, settled, and closely tied to the soil.
Its religion was bound to farming.
Its social and political order rested on landholding, aristocratic rank, and feudal bonds.
In all this it stood much nearer to the Tai, the Yi peoples of the southwest, the Mosuo, the Miao, and other southern peoples than to the cattle-herding nomads of the northern steppe.

The Chinese thus appear as the northernmost branch of a much wider world of sedentary agricultural peoples.
To the west stood the Tibeto-Burman peoples of Tibet, Sichuan, and Yunnan.
To the south stood the Tai of southern China and northern mainland Southeast Asia.
Between them stood the Miao groups of the central south.
Across much of what is now China, long before written history, many different peoples seem already to have shared some broad form of settled agrarian civilization.
The later spread of Chinese civilization to the south may therefore be seen not simply as conquest, but as the re-establishment in new form of a much older civilizational field.

sections.title: Life on the Northeastern Plain

paragraphs.text:
Life for these early Chinese may have been harsher than for their southern kindred.
Maspero imagines their civilization first taking shape in the great northeastern plain between the sea and the craggy wall of the Shanxi plateau.
From there it spread westward into the Wei valley, up the Fen, south toward the Huai and the Han, and eventually toward the road into the middle Yangtze world.

The climate was severe.
Summer could be torrid and winter glacial.
Just before spring came cutting winds loaded with sand, sometimes more trying than winter cold itself.
Rivers froze or filled with drifting ice in winter, then thawed suddenly and became torrents.
For a large part of the year communication was difficult.

The Yellow River, the great artery of the north, was never an easy road.
Its current ran fast.
Its bed was split by sandbanks.
Its branches wandered restlessly across the flat and almost level plain.
This was the old country of the Nine Rivers, where the river was said to divide into many channels.
Its course was then unlike the modern one, and after a long detour it reached the sea by way of the line later associated with the Hai River near modern Tianjin.

Each year the floods shifted the river and drove it into fresh beds.
Low ground turned into wide marshes, many now vanished and some surviving still.
Among them grew rushes and water plants.
Wild geese and cranes nested there.
Fish swarmed in the waters.
Elsewhere stood damp stretches of grassland broken by clumps of elm, wild plum, and chestnut.
This was not yet true forest.
Dense forest belonged mainly to the mountain margins of Shandong and Shanxi, where the domain of the non-Chinese peoples began.

The bush and marsh sheltered abundant game and dangerous beasts.
Tigers, leopards, bears, wild cattle, wild boar, deer, antelope, foxes, hares, rabbits, monkeys, and innumerable birds filled this half-cleared world.
The ancient winter hunt, with fire driven through the undergrowth, belongs to that landscape.
At the same time the better lands, once diked and worked, produced millet and sorghum in the north, rice south of the Yellow River, and wheat in many places.
Beans, gourds, indigo, hemp, mulberries, horses, and cattle all belonged to the same agricultural order.

sections.title: Fields, Hamlets, and Walled Manors

paragraphs.text:
In theory the cultivated countryside should have been ordered and almost bare of trees.
The land was imagined as divided into square units called jing, each about one li in area and itself divided into nine plots.
Eight families cultivated the outer plots for themselves and the ninth for the ruler as tax.
Whether this was ever fully realized in practice is another question, but it shows the ideal of a regulated agrarian order.

sections.title: Heroes Who Made the Land Habitable

paragraphs.text:
Because the work of clearing, draining, and taming the land was so ancient, later generations no longer remembered it as human labor alone.
They transferred it into the age when heaven first ordered the earth for human life.
Each region shaped the story according to its own terrain and fears.
Sometimes the obstacle was a flood.
Sometimes it was a mountain barrier.
Sometimes it was a monster whose defeat made agriculture possible.

In the northern plain the struggle took on a grand and violent form.
The Yellow Emperor, Huangdi, descended from heaven to set the world in order.
He had to fight Chiyou, a monstrous being with a bull's head and a serpent's body.
Chiyou tried to strike at the cosmic tree itself and plunge the world into darkness.
Huangdi answered him with armies of fierce beasts and with the Winged Dragon.
Chiyou summoned the powers of wind and rain.
Huangdi then brought down his daughter, the Goddess of Drought, whose mere presence dried the earth.
Chiyou was defeated and killed, and the world became habitable, though the goddess remained exiled in the northern wastes she had scorched.

From his body, after a marvel, Yu emerged.
Yu succeeded where his father had failed.

He opened passages through the mountains so that they could run off.

paragraphs.text:
Later Chinese historians did not leave these figures in the realm of myth.
They turned them into rulers and arranged them in sequence as though they formed the first history of mankind.
By the time the texts later gathered into the Shujing were taking shape, a connected narrative had already been assembled from legends, ritual memories, and court traditions.

Fu Xi was credited with the eight trigrams.
Nüwa instituted marriage.

The Chinese had spent many centuries creating the first rudiments of civilization in the great floodplain of the Yellow River.
They had slowly drawn away from neighboring peoples who remained outside that advance.
When they first emerge into clearer sight, around the eleventh or tenth century BC under the last Shang kings, they already possess a fairly advanced culture.

The king stands at the summit of this sharply ordered world.

When the king and his advisers disagree, the ancestors are consulted by divination.

The Shang royal house traced its origin to a miraculous birth.
The mother of Xie conceived after swallowing the egg of a bird, usually said to be a swallow.
Later tradition made Tang the Victorious the founder who overthrew the last ruler of the Xia and established a new dynasty.

Later descendants preserved the genealogy with care, and the traditional list agrees rather well with what can be gathered from the inscriptions.
The chronology, however, remains uncertain.

paragraphs.text:
Its core domain seems to have lain on both banks of the Yellow River, from the point where the river leaves the Shanxi highlands to the approaches of Taishan and the Huai basin.
Its capitals are remembered at Bo, then at Yin, identified with Xiaotun, and finally at Chaoge.
Beyond its directly ruled territory, the Shang kings exercised a wider suzerainty over much of the north and east.

sections.title: Western Colonization and the Rise of Zhou

paragraphs.text:
Around the middle or the end of the Shang age, Chinese farmers began to break out of the eastern plain and establish fresh domains at the expense of surrounding peoples.
They founded small states in the Huai mountains and pushed more decisively into the valleys of the Wei and the Fen.

paragraphs.text:
Several great lineages drove this movement, above all the Ji, the Si, and the Ying.
Members of these clans founded scattered principalities across the western marches, on both banks of the Yellow River, in southwestern Shanxi, in the Wei valley, and even beyond the Qinling into the Han valley.
The advance was not a single unified conquest but a gradual web of colonies, outposts, and noble houses.

Its families already dominated much of the country between the sea, Taishan, and the Yellow River.

The old Duke Danfu left the Jing valley and migrated south to the region of Qi on the Wei.

Tradition presents the Zhou victory as decisive.
The old Shang kingdom was broken up and redistributed.
The northern part, with the old capital and its dependent lands, was given to one royal brother and became the principality of Wei.
Farther east, another great block of territory was entrusted to the Duke of Zhou and became Lu.

This became Song.
The political center of gravity had passed away from them for good.

Both appear as great conquerors who extended Zhou power among the peoples of the four directions.
King Zhao is said to have died on campaign while crossing the Han River.

King Mu became the hero of an entire cycle of marvels.
He rides in a chariot drawn by horses of prodigious speed.
He travels to the sources of the Yellow River, reaches the mountain where the sun sets, and visits the Queen Mother of the West.
He marries a beauty met on campaign, is carried to the palace of the Yellow Emperor, and returns from heaven to find that almost no earthly time has passed.

After the first decades of consolidation, the Zhou kings of this age pushed outward with new energy and organized a larger imperial order.
King Mu in particular was remembered as a reformer of justice.

With King Xuan, authentic history begins to speak more clearly.
From his reign survive victory odes that celebrate actual expeditions.
They show a ruler trying to rebuild royal authority, restrain unruly vassals, and keep the surrounding peoples in check.

In 822 BC they had the audacity to plunder Hao itself while the king was away.
The royal army hurried in pursuit, overtook them at Taiyuan, and defeated them.

King You alienated the Count of Shen, whose daughter had been one of the chief royal consorts.
Dismissed and dishonored, that great lord allied himself with other malcontents and with non-Zhou forces.
They stormed Hao in 771 BC and killed the king.

One prince was set up in the west, another, Yijiu, was installed at Luoyi in the east.
Hao was too ruined to remain the center of the dynasty.

paragraphs.text:
The court of the Western Zhou should not be imagined in the polished and philosophical form that much later ritual texts liked to project back upon it.
Even in the ninth and eighth centuries, under Kings Xuan and You, it still retained something raw, violent, and half-savage beneath its outward pomp.

The king received the lords with solemn display.
He sat upon a raised dais facing south, with jade ornaments supporting his arms and dark hangings behind him.
At his left stood the minister assisting in the reception, and at his right the Grand Scribe.
The visiting lord entered, prostrated himself, remained at a distance in the middle court, and listened while the king spoke.
The minister repeated the royal words aloud, the scribe wrote them down at once, and the visitor prostrated himself again before withdrawing backward from the hall.

At the great ceremonies, above all at royal funerals, the dynasty displayed its treasure in full.
Precious stones, famous weapons, divining tortoise shells, the great drum, the royal seal, the red sword, and the pointed scepter of command were all brought out.
The effect was one of magnificence, but it was a magnificence still close to barbaric luxury.

Hunting was one of the chief occupations of the king and his nobles.
It was not merely amusement.
It was also a royal duty, because dangerous beasts still roamed in great numbers.
Vast drives were organized, the brush was burned to flush out game, and the king's party pursued buffalo, tigers, wild boars, wolves, and other animals with chariots and weapons.

Archery tournaments offered another regular diversion.

Like the hunt, they stood midway between religion, discipline, and pleasure.

The court drank millet wine in enormous quantity until the whole gathering was drunk, noisy, and disorderly.
The old poems show not a quiet refinement but shouting, staggering, caps slipping off, dishes overturned, and men dancing wildly long after all decorum had vanished.

paragraphs.text:
These violent entertainments offered only brief relief from the insecurity of court life.
Kings, consorts, courtiers, and ministers moved in a world of faction, suspicion, and sudden punishment.

King Li is said to have kept near him a sorceress from Wei who revealed by supernatural means which lords had spoken against him.
Those denounced were put to death at once.
The punishments could be savage.
A prince of Qi, accused of vilifying King Yi, was seized and boiled in a tripod.
Yet terror did not prevent faction.
King Li himself was driven from the capital by a court party and forced to flee.

And yet, for all this brutality, one is indeed watching the dawn of Chinese civilization.
Under the last kings of Western Zhou, literature began to rise in recognizable form.

sections.title: The Central Ministries of the Zhou Court

paragraphs.text:
As the empire expanded, the court had to enlarge the older royal administration.
The first Zhou kings seem largely to have inherited the Shang framework.
Later rulers adjusted it, and by the late Western Zhou, especially under Kings Xuan and You, the central system appears in a fairly developed form.
A reform of justice was attributed to King Mu.
Other changes were probably introduced later.
Around the eighth century the scribes even adopted a more cursive and less cumbersome official hand, the script later called zhuan.

timeline.caption: The administrative framework described here belongs above all to the western Zhou monarchy.

timeline.caption: Later tradition associated important legal and administrative reform with the age of King Mu.

timeline.caption: The shift to a more cursive official hand belongs to the late western Zhou effort to manage a growing bureaucracy.

paragraphs.text:
At the summit stood the prime minister.
He was the king's substitute in almost everything.
Under an energetic ruler he remained a great servant of the crown.
Under a weak or idle one he could become the real head of government.
That made the office a prize for powerful lineages.
It tended to gather in a few houses and could pass for long stretches through the same families.
Later ritual tradition would make the whole system look more symmetrical than it had been in life, but the political weight of the prime minister was real.

paragraphs.text:
Below him stood three first-rank ministers responsible for the broad conduct of the realm.
Later texts group them under several old collective names, but what matters is their actual function.
The Director of the Multitude, the ssu-tu, governed the common people in their civil life.
He supervised the allotment of fields, sowing, harvest, and threshing.
He directed corvee labor, sometimes in person.
He followed the peasantry even into the market, where police, prices, and places of sale fell under his authority.
Marriages, festivals, assemblies, and lesser legal proceedings among commoners also belonged to his sphere.

The Director of Horses, the ssu-ma, stood to the people of the royal domain in military matters as the Director of the Multitude stood to them in civil ones.
He called up levies, drilled them, reviewed them, and led them in war.
He presided over the great seasonal hunts, which were both military exercises and royal rites.
He controlled weapons, arsenals, chariots, horses, and the stud farms.
In victory he returned in triumph at the head of the troops, with flute in the left hand and axe in the right, and offered prisoners to the God of the Soil and to the ancestors.
In defeat he went into mourning.

The Director of Works, the ssu-kung, was concerned not with men but with land and things made upon it.
Fields, dikes, canals, uncultivated tracts, rivers, and mountains fell under him.
He maintained the great river dikes, planned canals, prevented silting, and supervised the smaller embankments that separated fields and served the periodic reallotment of land.
Artisans of every kind also belonged to his world, including architects, sculptors, founders, armorers, carpenters, and embroiderers.

Three other ministers, of slightly lower rank but hardly less importance, completed the core.
The Chamberlain managed the king's private sphere.
He saw to food, drink, fabrics, clothing, furniture, tools, stores, and treasure.
Butchers, cooks, dyers, furriers, shoemakers, storekeepers, eunuchs, and household domestics were subject to him.
Because he controlled both palace life and the royal treasury, his office tended in time to rise higher and higher.
In the royal court it could even absorb the older role of prime minister, though in the principalities it remained more simply the lord's household and financial office.

The Minister of Religious Affairs supervised the imperial cult, above all the cult of the ancestors.
Priests, prayer-sayers, augurs, diviners, interpreters of dreams, sorcerers, sorceresses, doctors, and veterinarians stood beneath him.
By the end of the dynasty even the great body of scribes seems to have been drawn into his sphere, though this may not have been so from the beginning.
The Director of Criminals oversaw the penal order of the state.
He stood over prisons, executioners, and the graver criminal procedures, while lesser civil authorities dealt with lighter cases.

Around these ministers stood a wider courtly ring.
There were exalted advisers such as the Grand Protector, the Grand Master, and probably also the Grand Guardian, figures later remembered together as the Three Dukes.
Their titles suggest very old functions, perhaps once tied to guiding the king through the dangerous taboos and sacred duties of his office.
There were also palace officials whose technical charge could be narrow but whose proximity to the king made them politically weighty.
The Grand Scribe and his whole college were especially important, since they wrote, preserved, and transmitted royal orders, legal texts, and ritual forms.

Later ritual books regularized this system into a more perfect and balanced pattern.
The heads of the six departments became the six ministers, and the whole arrangement acquired a symbolic symmetry suited to a weakened monarchy.
But while the royal institution still retained real substance, the central administration had to perform two very different tasks at once.
It managed empire-wide matters such as homage, tribute, war, and disputes among feudatories.
At the same time it administered the king's own domain.
That confusion was one of the permanent weaknesses of Zhou government.

notes.text: Modern study of bronze inscriptions confirms a substantial Western Zhou administrative apparatus, but the highly balanced six-ministry system of later ritual texts is partly schematic. Some of Maspero's reconstruction is plausible, yet the surviving contemporary evidence is more fragmentary than the transmitted manuals suggest.

sections.title: The Royal Domain and the Machinery of Local Rule

paragraphs.text:
The royal domain consisted first of the old family lands in the Wei valley, with Hao as western capital, and of the Luo valley and the middle Yellow River region, with Luoyi as the eastern capital.
Under the Eastern Zhou this domain shrank without cease.
After the catastrophe of 771 BC the kings never truly recovered the Wei valley.
The lands north of the Yellow River were eventually ceded to Jin.
What remained dwindled century after century until Qin absorbed the last remnant.

paragraphs.text:
Its organization was simple in outline but dense in detail.
Each capital and its suburbs formed a district that the king was considered to administer directly.
Around the capital lay the interior districts, where in theory no apanages were to be granted.
Beyond them stretched the exterior districts, many of which were entrusted to princes and officials.
The machinery in the two zones was much the same, though the divisions bore different names and the officers of the interior stood one degree higher than their counterparts outside.

notes.text: Excavated bronze inscriptions have strengthened the case that Western Zhou government already possessed real administrative offices rather than a purely ceremonial framework. Even so, the exact territorial grid and full hierarchy remain reconstructed rather than directly documented in complete form.

paragraphs.text:
In the inner zone the land was divided into regions.
In the outer zone it was divided into circles.
These larger units were subdivided into departments or districts, then into cantons or towns, then into commune-like units, and finally into villages or hamlets of twenty-five families.
At the top stood grand officers.
At the bottom stood lesser patrician chiefs.
The men who filled these posts were nobles, probably chosen in large part from the local aristocracy.
The highest bore the title of grand officer.
The humblest were simply men of the shih rank.

paragraphs.text:
Their work was extensive.
They made the regular sacrifices and presided over archery ceremonies.
They supervised the periodic reallotment of land, regulated agriculture, judged ordinary civil matters, oversaw plebeian marriages, directed the collection of taxes, and maintained the registry and census.
At the beginning of the year the prefects of regions and circles went to learn the new laws announced at the Sacred Palace, the Mingtang.
They then posted these in their own jurisdictions.
Their subordinates copied the procedure in turn.
For those who could not read, the regulations were also proclaimed aloud at the seasonal sacrifices to the God of the Soil.
At the end of the year every functionary had to render account to his superior.
Inspectors went the rounds of the jurisdictions and reported on what they found.

Beneath the administrators was a swarm of lesser officials.
There were go-betweens who handled peasant marriages under official supervision.
There were warehousemen in charge of the granaries where taxes in grain were stored.
Tax gatherers received dues after harvest and also made spring loans to the distressed.
Bursars ordered the issue of grain for sacrifices, visitors, troops on the move, and other needs.
Assessors fixed rates according to the productive value of the land.
Collectors drew in the dues owed from mountains and forests in timber and fuel.
Directors of markets maintained police, assigned places, and supervised taxation there.
Treasurers did for merchants what the tax gatherers did for peasants, taking dues on the one hand and advancing short loans on the other.

Above all, the local administration regulated agriculture with minute care.
It had fields demarcated and the small dikes and canals repaired.
It kept the peasants to the proper rhythm of sowing and harvest.
In summer it had the gates of towns and houses opened and suspended certain tolls.
In winter it closed everything again and saw that the peasants withdrew first into the villages and then into their houses.
It organized corvee labor and, when needed, military levies.
The peasant was followed by the state from the plot to the market, from marriage to taxation, and from the village assembly to the muster ground.

paragraphs.text:
Justice was divided between the ordinary civil administration and the criminal authorities.
Lesser offenses that did not require imprisonment were handled by local civil officials under the Director of the Multitude.
More serious matters belonged to the Director of Criminals and his subordinates.
Some magistrates traveled about correcting everyday faults such as contempt for elders, insults, quarrels, drunkenness, and other breaches of village order.
The usual punishment was flogging.
If a culprit repeated the offense, he could be treated as incorrigible and sent into the harsher criminal system.

Other itinerant officials tried to settle cases that could still be composed.
They dealt with accidental injuries, unintended killings, damage done by animals, legitimate self-defense, and even blood feuds.
Their aim was to reach an agreement between the parties before vengeance spread further.
When a settlement had been made, the guilty party received a tablet that protected him from renewed retaliation.
This was a society in which reconciliation and punishment stood side by side, and in which feud still remained a live possibility.

Serious criminal procedure was formal and elaborate.
Local provosts investigated and prepared the dossier.
Capital cases then went up to the Director of Criminals himself.
He heard them in open court together with the Deputy for Criminal Affairs and the assembled provosts of the jurisdictions concerned.
When sentence had been pronounced, it was written down in full, archived, and then carried back to the locality for execution.
The king appeared only if he wished to intervene with clemency.
Ordinary recidivists could meanwhile be exposed in the pillory in the palace court before being cast into prison.
The corpse of an executed criminal might remain displayed in the market for three days.

The penal code distinguished many grades of punishment.
The famous five chastisements were death, castration, amputation of the feet, cutting off the nose, and tattooing the face with black marks.
Some of these could be redeemed by large payments of copper, though only at a great cost.
The code also took account of circumstance.
An unpremeditated offense and a deliberate one were not weighed in the same way.
Thus even this ancient severity was not wholly blind.

There was no neat modern division between civil and criminal process.
A lawsuit easily became an accusation, and the losing party might be punished.
A man who opened proceedings brought with him a bundle of arrows and a bar of copper.
The other side had to answer with a corresponding deposit, or else appear to admit weakness.
When written agreements existed, the original text could be taken from the ancestral temple and compared with the claims of the parties.
If neither side could be proved right, both might be forced to swear and leave punishment to the gods.
Poor plaintiffs had their own recourse.
They stood by a special stone or beat the complaint drum at the palace gate until their grievance was heard.

Military organization repeated the civil hierarchy in another form.
Families supplied individual men.
Five families made a squad.
These small groups rose through larger and larger units until, in theory, the royal domain furnished six armies.
The total paper strength was immense, though not all such men would be called up at once.
The fundamental fighting element remained the war chariot, manned by nobles and supported by infantry.
Each contingent was led by the territorial chief who had raised it.
Thus civil and military command were closely interwoven.

An army on campaign marched and camped according to fixed rites.
At night the chariots were drawn into a barricade.
Tents were set up for the God of the Soil and for the royal ancestor whose tablet accompanied the host.
Only after divination had proved favorable did battle properly begin.
Even then, the two sides might spend time in formal provocations meant to draw the enemy into combat.
A warrior would ride up to the entrenchment, fire an arrow, insult the foe, seize a prisoner, or brush the camp and wheel away.
Drums gave the signal to advance and bells to retire.
Before the clash the commanders descended from their chariots to hear the general's harangue and to take part in the prayer.

Once fighting was joined, order quickly dissolved.
There was scarcely any strategy in the later sense.
The armies pressed straight ahead until they collided, and battle became a confused melee of chariots and foot soldiers.
Commanders challenged one another, exchanged ceremonious messages, and often fought almost as individuals.
The chief task of the general in the thick of battle was to keep the drum sounding.
Only toward the end of the Zhou period, when cavalry began to replace the old chariot arm, did more effective tactical command become possible.

Finance was the weakest point of the whole system.
A practical medium of exchange scarcely existed.
Taxes therefore had to be collected mainly in kind, in grain, fabric, timber, fodder, and other goods.
Cowry shells had long served as money, and for larger transactions men used copper ingots or measured cloth.
Only in the later centuries did cast coinage become common, in forms such as pierced discs, knife money, or spade money.
Even then taxes in kind remained the foundation of public revenue.

The chief levy was the land tax, effectively a tithe on the crop.
There were also dues on the produce of mountains and lakes, taxes on houses and enclosures, charges on apanages, fines, and market fees of many kinds.
But most of what was gathered never reached the center in a clean stream.
Local officials had first to maintain granaries, make loans, feed travelers and troops, stabilize markets, and meet ordinary expenditures.
The system thus consumed much of its own revenue before the surplus moved upward.
The Treasurer and Controller could watch accounts, but they had little direct hold over the local agents who gathered the taxes in the first place.
Leakage and abuse were built into the structure.

To simplify accounts, different revenues were assigned to different habitual expenses.
One stream maintained sacrifices.
Another supported visitors.
Another fed the court.
Another paid artisans or supplied fodder.
Daily life could be sustained after a fashion, but extraordinary burdens were far harder to meet.
War, famine, or major public works quickly exposed the weakness of the state.
In the later period the kings could no longer repair even their own walls without begging assistance from stronger feudatories.
The administrative apparatus was elaborate, but the financial base beneath it remained fatally thin.

sections.title: A Pattern Too Small for an Empire

paragraphs.text:
The royal administration, even when greatly enlarged, still resembled that of a rather small principality.
It assumed a ruler who was at once priest, civil head, and father of his subjects, able to supervise their lives closely because he stood near them.
Such a pattern, meticulous in detail yet weak in concerted management, was badly suited to a feudal empire spread across diverse lands, tongues, and customs.
The realm contained a crowd of autonomous petty lords who were often linked neither by habit nor by strong institutions.

timeline.label: Late Western Zhou

paragraphs.text:
In the eighth century the Yellow River basin was divided into at least a hundred little fiefs, not counting barbarian tribes that remained more or less independent.
The Royal Domain still occupied the center of the empire, in the lower Wei valley of Shaanxi and the Luo valley of Henan.
It was fertile and extensive, yet split in two by mountains.
The Yellow River, swift and difficult to navigate, was an unsatisfactory bond between the western and eastern halves, since one had to make a long detour before reaching Luoyi.

paragraphs.text:
In the west, along the upper Wei on the barbarian frontier, the small fiefs of Qin, Mi-hsü, and Juan, together with the duchy of Western Guo, were counted within the Royal Domain.
So too, probably, were the seigniories on the right bank of the Yellow River, such as Han, Rui, and Liang.
On the opposite bank, however, the principality of Yu already stood outside the domain.

paragraphs.text:
Farther north, near the mouth of the Fen, lay Wei and Geng.
Eastward up the Fen valley stood the small fief of Jin, still often called by its older name, Tang.
Still farther north were Zhao and Huo, close to the Di peoples who controlled the Ta-lu basin, later known as Taiyuan, and much of eastern Shanxi besides.

paragraphs.text:
Where the Yellow River emerged from the mountains, the great plain was divided among a new cluster of principalities.
North of the river stood Wey, the old Shang capital.
The districts of Yong and Bei were sometimes treated almost as separate dependencies of Wey itself.
South of the river, the descendants of the old Shang kings still retained part of their ancient land in the duchy of Song.

paragraphs.text:
West of Song, in the early eighth century, the domain of Zheng was detached from the Royal Domain and given to a brother of King Xuan.
To the south Song bordered Chen in the Huai mountains.
To the north it reached toward Cao, between the Yellow River and the Ji River.
To the northeast it met Lu, at the southern foot of Taishan, another important block carved from the former Shang realm.

East of Lu came a string of smaller fiefs, among them Zhu-lü, Ju, and Qu, bordering the Yi of Shandong.
North of Taishan, between the Yellow River and the sea, stood the powerful principality of Qi.
Farther north was Yan, in the region of present-day Beijing and at times extending toward southern Manchuria.
West of Qi lay smaller states such as Xing and the petty domains of the descendants of Fu Xi, including Ren and Hsü-gou.

Along the southern rim of the Huai mountains lay a chain of castles and little states, among them Chen, Cai, Xu, Dao, Jiang, Xi, and Xian.
Some had even crossed the mountains into barbarian country, such as Shen, Lü, Tang, and Sui.
Farther south, in the rich Hubei basin at the meeting of the Han and the Yangtze, the peoples of Chu were beginning to organize themselves into a Chinese-style kingdom.

sections.title: Princes, Vassals, and Titles

paragraphs.text:
The lords who answered directly to the king formed the feudal aristocracy and were called collectively the princes, the zhuhou.
One rank below them stood their own vassals, the fu-yung.
The title prince might suggest a neat uniformity, but the actual world of rank was more varied than that.
Most important lords were indeed called hou, which one may render as prince.
Yet several other titles circulated beside it, and old office, family prestige, ritual courtesy, and political habit all contributed to keep them alive.

paragraphs.text:
Some rulers, such as those of Qin, Zheng, and Cao, bore the title bo, count, because an ancestor had once held a local comital office and the designation had remained after the office itself had become largely nominal.
Others of essentially similar standing, such as Wey and Qi, preferred the title hou.
The king's great ministers bore the more exalted title gong, duke, and their descendants could retain it, as happened with the houses of Zhou and Guo.
The descendants of ancient sovereign lines also enjoyed it, as in Song, whose rulers descended from the former Shang kings, or in Chen and Qi, whose lines were linked in tradition to the ancient sage rulers.
By courtesy, moreover, all dead princes might be called gong when spoken of under their posthumous names.

paragraphs.text:
Chiefs of submitted barbarian peoples often bore the title tzu.
This was less a princely rank in the later sense than a dignified term of address, something like sire.
The ruler of Chu bore it.
In later centuries disciples would use the same word when speaking of their masters, as in Kongzi and Mozi.
Still lower in the later hierarchy stood nan, baron.
Yet the important thing is that these gradations were largely honorific.
They did not by themselves establish real political superiority.
A duke was not necessarily more powerful than a prince, nor a prince than a count.

paragraphs.text:
Ritual theory later arranged the titles in three levels.
Duke stood at the top.
Prince and count formed the middle rank.
Sire and baron stood at the bottom.
The distinction was reflected in the number of brevet dignities attached to each grade, nine for a duke, seven for a prince or count, and three for a sire or baron.
But this was a ritual language of precedence, not a true scale of power.
The feudal world remained too irregular for rank alone to define political weight.

sections.title: The Nine Provinces and Their Royal Pastors

paragraphs.text:
The Zhou kings attempted to impose some order upon this loose constellation of states by dividing the empire into nine provinces.
A late Western Zhou document, the Yugong, preserves the classic list.
To the north lay Ji, largely corresponding to southern Shanxi and bounded on west, south, and east by the Yellow River.
To the northeast lay Yan around the former mouth of the river in northern Hebei.
To the east lay Qing between the Yellow River and Taishan in northern Shandong.
Xu stretched southeastward from Taishan to the Huai and the coast.
Yang lay at the mouth of the Yangtze.
Jing occupied the middle Yangtze and lower Han.
Liang covered the upper Han.
Yong was the Wei valley.
At the center stood Yu, south of the Yellow River and along the Luo.

notes.text: The received Yugong should not be treated as a straightforward Western Zhou administrative document. Modern scholarship usually sees the extant text as later, with substantial Warring States shaping, even if it preserves older spatial and ideological traditions.

paragraphs.text:
The royal domain itself was divided between Yong and Yu, each containing one of the two capitals.
This matched the tradition that after the conquest King Wu divided the administration of the domain between two great figures, the Duke of Shao in the old western capital and the Duke of Zhou in the new eastern one.
Whether the arrangement was ever as neat in life as later theory liked to imagine, it expressed a real need.
The monarchy had to think provincially if it wished to govern a realm so broken in geography and in custom.

paragraphs.text:
In each province the king appointed a representative of royal authority from among the local lords.
He bore the title of count or pastor.
His duty was to maintain order, administer justice, punish rebels, and in general uphold the house of Zhou in that wider region.
A later document preserved in the archives of Qi, whether authentic or not, still shows how the office was understood.
The pastor was to punish the lords of the five ranks and the counts of the nine provinces when they were at fault, and so sustain the royal house.
The same text even defines the bounds of Qing by sea, river, mountain line, and northern limit.
That alone shows the breadth of the charge.

In the time of King Xuan the Prince of Shen was charged with holding back the barbarians of the south.
This likely means that he acted as pastor of Jing.
Around the same period the Prince of Qi watched the east, the Prince of Han the north, and the Prince of Lu the Hsü frontier.
These may correspond to similar provincial responsibilities in Qing, Yong, and Xu.
The arrangement had an obvious practical value.
The king could not be everywhere.
He therefore used great local houses as his arms and eyes in the provinces.
But this advantage was also a danger.
Those very men already had interests of their own.

sections.title: Royal Power and Its Limits

paragraphs.text:
That was the central weakness of the system.
By appointing provincial leaders from among the local lords, the kings gave royal office to men whose first loyalty could easily turn toward their own house.
So long as the monarchy appeared strong, the arrangement worked after a fashion.
The kings could still depose, punish, or replace troublesome feudatories.
But such interventions were intermittent and convulsive rather than steady and institutional.

timeline.caption: The limits of royal power become sharply visible in the last western Zhou century.

timeline.label: Sack of Hao
timeline.caption: The destruction of the western capital exposes the structural weakness of the whole feudal system.

paragraphs.text:
King Yi had the ruler of Qi arrested after accusations were brought against him and had him boiled in a tripod, then placed a younger brother on the throne.
A century later King Xuan put to death the usurper Bo-yu of Lu and gave the principality to another brother of the murdered lord.
Yet even such acts did not create lasting obedience.
King Xuan waited eleven years before punishing Bo-yu.
King Yi, after replacing one ruler of Qi with another, did nothing when the new one in turn was killed by a brother.
Royal authority could still strike, but it no longer held the whole field in a sustained grip.

The chief obligations of the lords were homage, tribute, and military service.
Later ritual theory represented these duties as if they had been regulated with clocklike regularity.
Reality seems to have been rougher.
Homage should in theory have been rendered every three, four, five, or six years according to distance, but actual attendance was much more irregular.
According to Lu tradition, a prince of that state did not go to court in person until 820 BC.
Even lords quite near the royal center neglected these visits at times.
When the Prince of Han had failed to appear in the fourth year of King Xuan, the king sent a great lord to summon him, and the delinquent came only after being frightened into obedience.

paragraphs.text:
Tribute was generally light in weight but rich in symbolic value.
It consisted of the characteristic products of each province, the things needed for ritual and court use.
Yan sent varnish and silk.
Qing sent salt, hemp, lead, and pine timber.
Xu sent pheasant plumes for dancers and sounding stones for musicians.
Yang and Jing sent metals, bamboo, ivory, skins, and useful woods.
Yu sent iron, silver, arrow-stone, and the skins of wild animals.
Yong sent jade.
Even barbarian peoples were expected to contribute what their lands yielded, such as felt, skins, or the silk of mountain mulberry.
A refusal to send tribute could be taken as rebellion.
This is why the failure of Chu to send its due offering of white grass could later serve as a political pretext for intervention.

paragraphs.text:
Seen as a whole, the Zhou empire of the eighth century looked much less like the perfect ritual order imagined by later theorists than like a loose and personal monarchy of the ancient world.
The king remained preeminent, but his power depended on force, prestige, and repeated proof.
Almost every ruler had to make that proof anew.
Sometimes the vassals even combined to unmake a king they found too energetic, too compromised by favorites, or simply too vulnerable.
A true unified state was still beyond reach.
Communications were difficult.
Population was sparse.
Non-Zhou peoples still occupied the spaces between provinces.
The Zhou kings were pursuing a dream larger than the conditions of their age could yet sustain.
